To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Federal Circuit and the district courts are applying claim differentiation in a similar manner, and that there are two primary ways that claim differentiation can lead to bad results:

(1) the doctrine of claim construction is used in 25% of the cases decided in the district courts and 50% of the cases in the Federal Circuit, (2) in the vast majority of the cases, the doctrine is used in a manner that is consistent with the doctrine of claim interpretation, (3) there is little consistency in the application of the doctrine of claim differentation, (4) the doctrine is most frequently used by the Federal Circuit, and the district courts,

the doctrine of claim distinction has been used by courts to limit the scope of broad claims to the preferred range of embodiments disclosed in the patent, and this use of the doctrine has been problematic in a substantial number of cases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) how often is claim differentiation used in patent litigation; (2) how often is it used to broaden a patent claim; and (3) how often is its use appropriate.
the following question: What are the appropriate boundaries of the doctrine of claim construction, in light of the doctrine of patent claim differentiation?
the following questions: (1) How is claim differentiation being applied?; (2) What are the consequences of claim differentiation?; and (3) How can we better limit the doctrine?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the doctrine should only be applied when the claims at issue are not coextensive, the claims at issue have different limitations, and the claims at issue do not have a common disclosure.
the claim differentiation doctrine should be used to prevent defendants who are improperly seeking to narrow broader genus claims to embodiments actually disclosed or recited in the specification.
courts should not use the doctrine of claim differentation to prevent a claim from being limited to a range of embodiments that would otherwise be obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the doctrine of claim construction is an important tool that should be used to prevent defendants’ attempts to improperly narrow broad claims.
claim differentiation is most appropriate when used to prevent defendants or courts from limiting broad genus claims to the embodiments disclosed in more specific claims.
the doctrine of claim differentiaiton is a powerful and important interpretive tool, but it is not an all purpose solution for every interpretive problem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
claim differentiation is most appropriately used when it is clear from a reading of the specification that a broad genus claim is not intended to include all embodiments of a disclosed invention.

claim differentiation is most useful when applied to claims that have the same or similar limitations, but it is not appropriate to use the doctrine to broaden claims when they differ in important ways.
the claim differentiation doctrine should not be applied to prevent a claim from being interpreted in light of the specification when the specification clearly discloses the invention in the claim.
